channel.title: MIT News - Artificial intelligence
channel.description: MIT news feed about: Artificial intelligence

item.title: Why teaching AI about symmetry could make prenatal diagnosis more reliable
item.description: A model developed by researchers at MIT and Boston Children's Hospital adjusts scans on the fly to track fetal movement, potentially sparing families repeat hospital visits.

item.title: Giving AI a “crystal clear” view of the materials world
item.description: New research can help AI models understand crystalline materials in 3D and reason about their properties.

item.title: Fostering community amid Kendall Square’s innovation
item.description: The 18th annual Kendall Square Association Annual Meeting explored how new technologies could be a force for shared prosperity in society.

item.title: State of Supply Chain Sustainability Report finds corporate commitment at record high, but governance lags behind
item.description: MIT's Center for Transportation and Logistics finds sustainability commitments are strong, but governance gaps and external disruptions prevent execution.

item.title: AI model decodes the language cells use to communicate
item.description: A new computational approach reveals how cells communicate to assemble into tissues. This could accelerate stem cell engineering, improve disease models, and inform therapies.

item.title: Q&A: The “collision” between AI, your brain, and society
item.description: In a new book, Professor Eric So explores how the technology affects our thinking skills.

item.title: Researchers improve weather forecasts looking two to six weeks out
item.description: A new machine-learning approach broke records for weather forecasting for an important time frame in emergency planning.

item.title: How artificial neural networks build their own learning machinery
item.description: Machine-learning networks can learn without detailed instructions from a designer. Those that do may offer insight into how the brain reorganizes itself during learning.

item.title: MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosts National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology
item.description: Roadshow event highlights Massachusetts' defense-biotechnology ecosystem.

item.title: Q&A: Building accountability behind our words — and AI’s — in civic conversations
item.description: Professor Deb Roy contends there should be someone who is “answerable” for every piece of text in public life, no matter its origins.

item.title: 3 Questions: What is the best path forward for AI in academia?
item.description: MIT Statistics and Data Science Center Director Alexander (Sasha) Rakhlin shares important considerations for departments and institutions.

item.title: Using AI to mitigate the growing environmental threat of data centers
item.description: By rethinking how large cloud computing systems operate, Associate Professor Christina Delimitrou seeks to make data centers more energy efficient.

item.title: Discovering the value of humanistic inquiry
item.description: Students in MIT’s Concourse program delve deeply into the human condition, debate challenging questions, and learn to develop judgment about issues that can’t be quantified.

item.title: Supercomputing researchers document evolution of AI hardware
item.description: An ongoing survey tracks the latest AI accelerator systems to keep hardware relevant for Lincoln Laboratory staff and sponsors.

item.title: Chris Bourg named vice provost and Barbara K. Ostrom (1978) Director of the MIT Libraries
item.description: As director, Bourg has focused on digital access, open and equitable scholarly publishing, and expanded support for data-intensive research.

item.title: MIT announces the MIT for America initiative, to strengthen STEM education across the country
item.description: The effort aims to help U.S. learners from kindergarten to community college, with an emphasis on math, making, and the constructive use of AI.

item.title: Computational tools for society’s most complex challenges
item.description: Associate Professor Cathy Wu uses reinforcement learning to help map out improvements to transportation and other multifaceted systems.

item.title: Documenting the tech worker movement
item.description: Writing as a participant and researcher, PhD student JS Tan SM ’22 has co-authored a new book about the rise of tech worker protests and the employer backlash that followed.

item.title: 3 Questions: A new resource to empower young entrepreneurs
item.description: Martin Trust Center Managing Director Bill Aulet introduces Dear Dreamer, a free platform for middle and high school students who want to learn about entrepreneurship.

item.title: New tool lets users repair AI-generated 3D models, then fabricate them just the way they want
item.description: “InstructMesh” can generate designs for everyday objects that are easy to edit and fabricate for both experts and newcomers to 3D modeling.

item.title: MIT Transit Lab to develop an AI platform for public transit agencies
item.description: With $2.1 million funding from Google.org, the open-source Public Transit Intelligence Hub will unify public transit monitoring, operations, and passenger communication.

item.title: This game-playing AI is the new champ at Stratego
item.description: Able to defeat top-ranked human players and more efficient than other models, the new system could help decision-makers in military maneuvers or business negotiations.

item.title: The effects of an “algorithmic monoculture” depend on the details
item.description: In a study focusing on hiring decisions, MIT researchers found the use of a single algorithm by many firms could benefit job seekers in certain situations.

item.title: Who we become when we talk to machines
item.description: Professor Sherry Turkle’s new book, “Artificial Intimacy,” offers a withering critique of chatbots and the antisocial dynamics she believes they encourage.

item.title: New formulation helps RNA vaccines withstand high temperatures
item.description: MIT engineers have found a way to stabilize the lipid nanoparticles used to deliver RNA vaccines, which could allow the vaccines to be more widely distributed.

item.title: MIT students gain a humanist lens on technical innovation in Tulsa, Oklahoma
item.description: The PKG Center for Social Impact expands Code.Tulsa experiential learning program.

item.title: Estimating suicide risk from text
item.description: A new language-processing tool could help identify the highest-risk individuals from natural language, enabling swifter interventions.

item.title: The promise and peril of using visual AI to study cities
item.description: In their new book, “How AI Sees the City,” the leaders of MIT’s Senseable City Lab examine the technology’s implications for researching urban life.

item.title: MIT welcomes David Siegel SM ’86, PhD ’91 as its next Innovation Fellow
item.description: Computer scientist, entrepreneur, and philanthropist will collaborate with the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing to advance AI and scientific discovery.

item.title: Poitras Center to fuel early careers of 50 young scientists dedicated to psychiatric disorders research
item.description: Patricia and James Poitras ’63 provide fellowships for graduate students and postdocs who will shape the future of mental health research.

item.title: A new chapter for MIT Reads
item.description: A new focus on fiction and memoir aims to help the MIT community celebrate the power of storytelling and strengthen social connection.

item.title: New AI technique could make minimally invasive surgeries safer and more precise
item.description: This patient-specific method, called xvr, helps doctors use X-rays for surgical navigation in fields such as orthopedics and neurosurgery.

item.title: Measure by measure, studying society accurately
item.description: Naoki Egami has become a standout in political methodology, helping refine tools that give scholars durable results.

item.title: New method enables AI for safety-critical situations
item.description: The “HardFlow” algorithm could help generative AI models produce high-quality outputs that obey strict requirements when “pretty close” doesn’t cut it.

item.title: MIT spinout turns plastic waste into resilient building materials
item.description: Atlas Building Composites is commercializing MIT research to turn plastic waste into parts for buildings and other infrastructure.

item.title: Lifesaving Lincoln Laboratory device wins 2026 Excellence in Technology Transfer Award
item.description: The handheld catheterization device AI-GUIDE, created by Lincoln Laboratory and Massachusetts General Hospital, promises improved health outcomes for injured service members and civilians.

item.title: MIT Schwarzman College of Computing launches pilot to help educators teach AI across disciplines
item.description: A weeklong summer workshop brought higher education faculty to campus to explore how AI and machine learning materials can be adapted for their classrooms.

item.title: From MIT to IBM, expediting AI and quantum deployment
item.description: MIT affiliates engage with the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab to bring rigorous theory to production systems.

item.title: System helps humans predict when self-driving cars will make mistakes
item.description: A new method, called CW-Net, translates the reasoning process of an autonomous vehicle’s AI system into understandable concepts that explain its behavior.

item.title: Walter Torous named executive director of MIT Center for Real Estate
item.description: The senior lecturer, already director of the degree program, will now oversee all aspects of the center’s activities and operations.

item.title: Ila Kumar: Innovating with communities
item.description: The PhD student works to give young people an active role in shaping digital technologies that can support their own well-being.

item.title: MIT Quantum Initiative launches postdoctoral fellowship program
item.description: The Institute welcomes its first cohort of QMIT Fellows this fall to advance interdisciplinary quantum research.

item.title: How an MIT research project became a global programming language
item.description: With millions of users across the world, Julia has been used to conduct cutting-edge research and to design new drugs, jet engines, heat pumps, and more.

item.title: Looking beyond natural sequences
item.description: A new machine-learning framework aims to improve the success rate of computational protein design while moving away from results that reproduce sequences found in nature.

item.title: AI helps design new materials that work in the real world
item.description: The “CrysVCD” tool developed at MIT could cut the huge amounts of time and money spent on screening out chemically unstable designs.

item.title: Generating scenarios for extreme events, without extreme data
item.description: A new algorithm learns to anticipate the unprecedented scenarios that critical infrastructure and global supply chains are least prepared for.

item.title: Paving the way for greener ammonia production
item.description: New MIT research could lead to better materials for a fossil-fuel-free process for making the chemical that's essential to fertilizer and other products.

item.title: When AI art has no author: Study finds generated images often can’t be traced to training data
item.description: A new method for surgically removing training examples from a model reveals that as datasets grow, the link between what a model learns and what it produces dissolves.

item.title: With a feel for physics, AI models simulate a wider range of real-world scenarios
item.description: “GeoPT” helps AI models understand the basics of physics so they can simulate how objects respond to things like wind and water more efficiently and accurately.

item.title: The benefits of medical AI assistance vary based on user expertise
item.description: Study finds non-experts deferred to LLM-based diagnostic assistance, even when it was wrong, while clinicians caught AI errors.
